title: Routers hijacked, management servers exposed, directory admins conjured
paragraphs: Good morning, it's 5:22 AM. It's Monday, the seventh of September, twenty twenty-six. 522 AM is brought to you by Lab522, a technology partner for mid-market businesses, providing cyber security services and enterprise operational software. Email hello at lab522 dot co dot uk if you think we can help your business. Attackers are chaining two recently disclosed MikroTik RouterOS flaws to take over routers with SSH exposed to the internet, and that's the sort of foothold that comes with an excellent view of everything behind it.

The chain includes an SSH authentication bypass, and MikroTik released a patch late last week. SANS ISC's advice is blunt: assume compromise. If you run RouterOS with internet-facing SSH, apply the vendor's patch and investigate the router rather than treating the update as a clean bill of health. The safe release number isn't specified, so check MikroTik's advisory before choosing the upgrade.

That management foothold gets considerably bigger with N-able N-central, the remote monitoring and management platform used to look after fleets of machines. Every on-premises build below 2026 point 3 point 1 point 14 needs Hotfix Four for an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw rated ten out of ten. Yes, that includes servers given Hotfix Three a day earlier: yesterday's emergency work doesn't get you over today's line.

N-able's incident notice says it's been exploited in the wild; its release notes call that unconfirmed. That's a contradiction, not a reason to wait. Code execution on the server managing other servers puts the management fleet in the blast radius, so I'd get Hotfix Four onto affected on-premises installations and investigate possible compromise alongside the upgrade.

While we're on remote management, ScreenConnect has two separate problems worth keeping separate. A worm-like campaign uses backdoored ScreenConnect instances and modified clients to transfer and execute payloads on newly connected systems, including a four-stage VBScript chain. The connection you use to help a machine becomes the delivery route for infecting it. Check newly connected hosts for unexpected transfers and script execution, and validate the ScreenConnect software doing the connecting.

Separately, ConnectWise has disclosed a new ScreenConnect Remote Access vulnerability, with a patch planned for later this week and temporary mitigations available now. Don't assume that flaw explains the campaign; no connection between them has been established here. If you operate ScreenConnect Remote Access, use ConnectWise's current mitigation notice while waiting for the fix.

Remote execution is also landing on shopfronts: attackers are exploiting the StyleSmuggler zero-day to execute code and plant a stealthy backdoor in Adobe Commerce and Magento stores. That's a foothold inside the application serving your customers, not merely a defaced page. Affected releases and a fix aren't clear yet, so check vendor guidance and investigate unexpected code changes and backdoors rather than waiting for visible damage.

And attackers don't need a server exploit if they can get through the identity front door. BigBear two point zero, a phishing-as-a-service framework, has bypassed MFA at two hundred and fifty-eight organisations and stolen more than five thousand Microsoft three sixty-five credentials. The bypass mechanism hasn't been described, so don't casually label it an adversary-in-the-middle attack. For investigations involving that service, an MFA-protected account isn't evidence that the access was legitimate.

There's a related trap in the JSCeal malware findings: it can bypass Google authentication using stolen session cookies. This is compiled V8 JavaScript malware with credential harvesting, surveillance and traffic-interception capabilities. If JSCeal is found on an endpoint, include Google session exposure in the investigation, not just stolen passwords. A live session is already through the door.

Which makes today's new directory flaws particularly uncomfortable: one doesn't even need to steal a session. CVE-2026-18922 affects three-eight-nine Directory Server, the LDAP server behind Red Hat Directory Server, with Red Hat Directory Server eleven and twelve identified. An attacker attempts a SASL PLAIN bind as Directory Manager with the wrong password, then completes a SASL ANONYMOUS bind on the same connection. A stale identity survives from the failed attempt and is installed after the successful anonymous bind, granting Directory Manager authority without valid credentials.

That's an authentication failure with a very literal punchline: wrong password, right administrator. It's nine point eight, reachable over the network with no login and no click, and the prize is control of the directory that other services trust. If you run those Red Hat Directory Server releases, prioritise checking the vendor advisory and controlling access to LDAP while establishing the fix. A directory administrator isn't automatically root on every client, but control of the identity store is quite enough trouble.

The neighbouring flaw attacks the same trust from FreeIPA, Red Hat's identity server, the thing handing out Kerberos tickets to Linux machines across the network. CVE-2026-76578 is missing authentication in the access rule for self-managed OTP tokens, which also fails to limit the attributes added with a token entry. Combined with a separately tracked directory-server access-rule evaluation flaw, an anonymous LDAP client can create an attacker-controlled Kerberos principal and put it in the administrators group.

Again, nine point eight: network access, no credentials, no click. This isn't just permission to enrol a token; the chain creates a new administrator inside the identity service. Red Hat Enterprise Linux seven and ten are identified, but exact affected builds and fixed versions for these directory issues aren't clear yet. If you operate FreeIPA there, check both sides of the chain with Red Hat rather than assuming a token-setting change alone closes it.

Identity infrastructure isn't the only trusted intermediary needing attention. Dell Secure Connect Gateway is the support gateway connecting enterprise equipment to Dell's support services, and CVE-2026-61410 lets an unauthenticated remote attacker send a crafted request that bypasses authorisation and executes commands on the target system. It's nine point four, over the network with no login and no click. That places the attacker inside the support gateway's environment; how far that reaches depends on what the gateway can access.

For Secure Connect Gateway five point zero, update the appliance from anything before 5 point 36 point 00 point 16 to that release or later. For the application edition, the threshold is 5 point 36 point 00 point 00. Dell recommends upgrading at the earliest opportunity, and with command execution needing no account, that's a sensible place to spend the maintenance window.

Back at the network edge, don't confuse a public exploit with confirmed exploitation, but don't ignore it either. CVE-2026-86296 is a stack-based buffer overflow in the D-Link DIR-822A's udhcpcd component, specifically strcpy in serverpacket dot c, affecting A underscore 101. It's rated ten, remotely reachable with no credentials and no click, and an exploit is public. The established mechanism is stack corruption, putting the router's integrity and availability at risk; code execution isn't explicitly confirmed, and no safe firmware release is identified.

A diagnostic tool becomes a command launcher on the Linksys RE7000 range extender running 2 point 0 point 15. CVE-2026-86299 injects operating-system commands through the PingTest handler's IP address, packet-size or repetition parameters. It's nine point nine, reachable over the network with a low-privilege account and no click, with a public exploit. That gives an attacker commands on a device inside the network; check vendor remediation guidance and limit management access, because a fixed release hasn't been identified.

The industrial version of that story is Advantech's WISE-6610 family, gateways sitting between LoRaWAN devices and their network services. Two public command-injection exploits affect firmware 1 point 2 point 1 underscore 20251110 across the WISE-6610 and WISE-6610-EL NB, EB, TB, JB and CB variants, plus WISE-6610P DEA, DNA and DTA. Both score nine point nine and need network access plus a low-privilege account, but no click. Both manipulate an argument called act, turning a gateway management action into attacker-chosen commands on the gateway.

One is in Basic Station certificate deletion; the other is in the Node-RED library handler. For the Node-RED flaw, CVE-2026-79698, upgrade to 1 point 2 point 4 underscore 20260821. That fix is confirmed for the Node-RED issue, not for the certificate-deletion flaw, so verify coverage before closing both tickets. The gateway's position between field devices and upstream services makes this more consequential than an ordinary web form accepting the wrong input.

That distinction between a scary headline and actual exposure matters for Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX, the web-component toolkit embedded in business applications. TantoSec has released a proof of concept chaining an AES-CBC padding oracle into unauthenticated remote code execution, but only in a specific non-default application configuration. Progress patched the chain in July. If you own an application using the toolkit, check its configuration and whether it includes that July fix; public exploit code makes the work timely, but not every Telerik deployment is exposed.

There's less qualification on the access requirements for Next4Biz CSM, a customer-service management application. CVE-2026-7861 is untrusted-data deserialisation allowing code injection in releases through the date-coded version 07092026. It's nine point eight, over the network with no login and no click, putting the application's code and the customer-service data it handles at risk. The vendor didn't respond to the disclosure contact and no fix is identified, so affected operators need a remediation answer and should review whether the application must remain broadly reachable.

Code running where it shouldn't also features in a North Korean Linux espionage campaign targeting automotive and media organisations in South Korea. The toolkit embeds a backdoor in HAProxy, the proxy and load balancer often sitting directly in the request path, for long-term surveillance. If you're investigating those environments, include HAProxy binaries and deployment changes in integrity checks. Looking only for an unfamiliar process can miss malware wearing a very familiar name.

The breach stories underline how much exposure sits behind the main service. Mathspace, the online maths learning platform, says attackers stole data concerning more than a million students, staff and parents after compromising its internal Metabase reporting system. Metabase is the analytics tool used to query and present business data: the reporting layer was the route into the records. If you operate a comparable reporting service, review its exposure and the data its connections can read; the exact intrusion mechanism at Mathspace hasn't been disclosed.

That dependency problem extends beyond software you host. Trezor says the August breach at shipping and logistics provider ShipMonk affects an additional sixty-seven thousand US customers, bringing the total to eighty-one thousand. This is a logistics-provider breach, not evidence that Trezor hardware wallets were compromised. Affected customers should use Trezor's breach communications to establish their exposure, without treating a shipping-data incident as proof that wallet secrets were taken.

I'd put exposed MikroTik routers and affected on-premises N-central servers at the front of the queue, with investigation running alongside remediation. I'd then check the directory services and Dell gateway versions, and keep a close eye on ConnectWise's promised patch this week. 522 AM, brought to you by Lab522. Find us at lab522 dot co dot uk.
